title: Claude for Agency Operations: the plug-and-play system that replaces junior ops work (SOPs, onboarding, capacity)

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.html:
Most agency onboarding looks like this: the intake form lands, someone downloads it, then re-types the same answers into one Claude chat for the fundamentals doc, another for the LinkedIn branding, another for the prospecting scripts. Each chat has its own prompt living in one person's head.

At two clients a week, that is roughly 100 minutes of senior time, weekly, on copy-paste work. It also freezes the day the founder travels, because the prompts and the judgment never got written down.

The fix is to turn each Claude project into a skill: one instruction file, one repeatable input, one finished deliverable. Same prompts, same examples, same voice, every time, run by anyone.

The win is not a faster chat. The win is that onboarding stops depending on who is awake.

sections.title: How the system is wired
sections.html:
One intake fills a shared brief. Six skills read that brief and each writes its own document. An orchestrator agent runs them in sequence so a new client goes from form to first-cut package without a human re-typing anything.

StepManual todayWith the skill system
Intake to fundamentalsDownload form, paste into Claude project ABrief auto-fills; onboarding-fundamentals writes the doc
Action briefRe-type into project Baction-brief reads the same brief
LinkedIn brandingRe-type into project Clinkedin-branding drafts headline + about
Prospecting / DM scriptsRe-type into project Dmicro-offers writes the outreach
Capacity checkFriday gut-feelcapacity-planner returns a number
SOP for the new repeatableNever written downsop-from-transcript drafts it from a call

Time cost before: ~50 minutes of senior work per client. After setup: about 4 minutes of review per deliverable. Who can run it: anyone on the team, founder optional.

sections.title: The shared brief (fill this once)
sections.html:
Every skill reads from one block. Paste your intake answers into this and keep it at the top of the project.

# CLIENT BRIEF, single source of truth
Client name:
Website:
Industry:
Team size:
Target audience (who they sell to):
Top 3 problems they solve:
Their offer(s) and rough price band:
Tone they want (e.g. plain, warm, direct):
Words/claims to avoid:
Proof they can cite (results, numbers, named wins):
Primary goal for next 90 days:
Notes / anything unusual:

sections.title: The 5 skills
sections.html:
Each block is a complete SKILL.md. Frontmatter name + description, then the instructions. Save each under its own folder.

Skill 1, onboarding-fundamentals

---
name: onboarding-fundamentals
description: Use right after intake. Turns the CLIENT BRIEF into a one-page fundamentals document (name, site, audience, problems solved, positioning).



# Role
You write the client fundamentals doc that every later deliverable depends on.


# Input
Read the CLIENT BRIEF block at the top of the project. If a field is blank,
list it under "Open questions" at the end. Do not invent facts.


# Output (exact order)

  1. Client at a glance: name, website, industry, team size.
  2. Who they serve: one tight paragraph naming the buyer.
  3. Problems they solve: 3 bullets, each a real pain in the buyer's words.
  4. Positioning line: one sentence the client could say out loud.
  5. Proof points: pull only from the brief's proof field.
  6. Open questions: every blank field, as a checklist.

# Rules

  • Plain sentences. No filler openers.
  • Every claim traces to a brief field. If it is not in the brief, it goes
  in Open questions, never in the body.

  • One page. If it runs longer, cut adjectives first.

Skill 2, action-brief

---
name: action-brief
description: Use after fundamentals. Produces the 90-day action brief: goal, the 3-5 moves that get there, and what the agency owns vs the client.



# Role
You convert the fundamentals doc into a 90-day plan the team can execute.


# Input
The fundamentals doc and the CLIENT BRIEF "Primary goal" field.


# Output

  1. Goal restated as one measurable outcome (number + date).
  2. The 3 to 5 moves that reach it, ranked by impact.
   For each move: what it is, why it matters, who owns it, week it starts.

  1. Dependencies: anything that must exist before a move can start.
  2. First-week actions: 3 concrete tasks, each assignable today.

# Rules

  • Every move has a named owner (Agency or Client). No "we" without a name.
  • Rank by impact, highest first. Say why the top move is top in one line.
  • If the goal has no number, write the best measurable proxy and flag it.

Skill 3, linkedin-branding

---
name: linkedin-branding
description: Use for client LinkedIn setup. Drafts a headline and an about section in the client's voice from the brief.



# Role
You write the client's LinkedIn headline and about section.


# Input
CLIENT BRIEF: audience, problems solved, offer, tone, proof.


# Output

  1. Headline: 3 options, each under 220 characters, buyer-outcome first.
  2. About section: 4 short paragraphs.
   - Open with the buyer's problem in their words.
   - State what the client does and for whom.
   - One proof paragraph using only brief proof points.
   - Close with a plain next step (how to reach them).

  1. Voice check: 2 lines confirming tone matches the brief's "Tone" field.

# Rules

  • Match the brief's tone field exactly. If it says plain, stay plain.
  • Use only proof that appears in the brief.
  • No hype verbs. Write what the client actually does, in real words.

Skill 4, micro-offers

---
name: micro-offers
description: Use for outreach setup. Writes the DM / prospecting scripts and the micro-offer the client opens conversations with.



# Role
You write the client's cold outreach: opener, follow-ups, and a micro-offer.


# Input
CLIENT BRIEF: audience, problems solved, offer, proof, tone.


# Output

  1. Micro-offer: one low-friction thing the buyer says yes to (audit, teardown,
   sample). One sentence, framed as the buyer's gain.

  1. Opening DM: under 400 characters, references a real buyer problem, ends with
   one soft question.

  1. Two follow-ups: each adds a new angle or proof point. No "just bumping this".
  2. One objection reply: for the most common brush-off in this niche.

# Rules

  • Lead every message with the buyer's situation, not the client's pitch.
  • One ask per message. Never stack two questions.
  • Keep it human. Short words, no template smell.

Skill 5, capacity-planner

---
name: capacity-planner
description: Use weekly or before taking a new client. Returns how many onboardings the team can absorb this week, as a number with the math shown.



# Role
You answer one question: how many new clients can we onboard this week
without overloading the team?


# Input (ask for any that are missing)

  • Senior hours available for onboarding this week (H)
  • Hours one onboarding now takes with the skills (T)
  • Onboardings already committed this week (C)

# Math
Free capacity = floor(H / T) - C


# Output

  1. The number, stated plainly: "Room for N more this week."
  2. The math, one line, with the inputs filled in.
  3. If the number is 0 or negative: name the single move that frees the most
   hours (usually raising T's automation share), and the hours it returns.

  1. A one-line trend note if prior weeks were given.

# Rules

  • Always show the arithmetic. A number with no math is a guess.
  • Round down. Never promise capacity you cannot prove.

sections.title: The pre-built agents
sections.html:
Skills hold the instructions. Agents run them. Below is an orchestrator that fires the onboarding sequence end to end, plus the per-step worker pattern. Drop these in .claude/agents/ (Claude Code) or describe them as roles inside a project.

---
name: onboarding-orchestrator
description: Runs a full new-client onboarding from a filled CLIENT BRIEF. Calls each skill in order and assembles one package.
tools: Read, Write



You run new-client onboarding start to finish.


Sequence (stop and surface blockers, do not invent missing facts):

  1. Confirm the CLIENT BRIEF has every field. If any are blank, list them and
   ask before continuing.

  1. Run onboarding-fundamentals. Save output as 01-fundamentals.md.
  2. Run action-brief using that output. Save as 02-action-brief.md.
  3. Run linkedin-branding. Save as 03-linkedin.md.
  4. Run micro-offers. Save as 04-outreach.md.
  5. Run capacity-planner for the current week. Save as 05-capacity.md.
  6. Write a one-page index listing each doc and its open questions.

Rule: every doc traces back to a brief field. Anything unsupported goes in
that doc's open-questions list, never in the body.


---
name: deliverable-worker
description: Generic runner for a single onboarding skill. Pass it one skill name and the brief; it returns one finished, reviewed deliverable.
tools: Read, Write



You produce exactly one deliverable, then stop.


Steps:

  1. Read the named skill's instructions and the CLIENT BRIEF.
  2. Produce the deliverable in the skill's exact output order.
  3. Self-check before returning:
   - Every claim traces to a brief field.
   - Output order matches the skill spec.
   - No hype verbs, no template openers.

  1. Return the deliverable plus a 2-line "what I assumed" note.

If a required brief field is blank, stop and ask. Do not fill gaps with
plausible-sounding detail.

An agent that runs the step beats a prompt that describes it. The worker does the self-check you would otherwise do by eye at 11pm.

sections.title: Plug-and-play prompts (paste and go)
sections.html:
No project setup needed. Drop the brief in and run these directly.

SOP from a process you already do:

You are writing a standard operating procedure for an agency team.

Here is a description of how we do [PROCESS NAME] today:
[PASTE your rough description or bullet notes]


Write the SOP with these sections, in order:

  1. Purpose: one line on what this produces and why.
  2. When to run it: the trigger.
  3. Inputs needed: every file, login, or piece of info, as a checklist.
  4. Steps: numbered, each starting with an action verb, each doable by a new hire.
  5. Definition of done: how we know the output is correct.
  6. Common failure: the one thing that breaks most often and the fix.

Rules: plain language, one action per step, no jargon a new hire would miss.
Flag anything I left vague as "[CLARIFY: ...]" instead of guessing.

Weekly capacity check:

Tell me how many new clients my team can onboard this week.

Inputs:

  • Senior hours free for onboarding this week: [H]
  • Hours one onboarding now takes: [T]
  • Onboardings already committed: [C]

Compute: floor(H / T) minus C.
Return: the number in plain words, then the math on one line with my inputs
filled in. If it is zero or negative, name the single change that frees the
most hours and how many hours it returns. Round down.

Voice-match pass (run on any draft before it ships):

Here is a client deliverable draft:
[PASTE draft]

Here is the client's tone and banned words from the brief:
Tone: [paste]
Avoid: [paste]


Rewrite only what breaks tone or uses a banned word. Keep everything else
untouched. Return the corrected draft, then a 3-line list of what you changed
and why. Do not add new claims.

sections.title: The SOP builder (writes the doc from a transcript)
sections.html:
This is the piece that ends "the process lives in one person's head." Hand it a call recording transcript and it returns a finished SOP. Ship it as a skill so anyone can run it.

---
name: sop-from-transcript
description: Turns a raw call or screen-share transcript into a finished SOP. Use after recording yourself doing a process once.



# Role
Someone narrated or screen-shared a process. You turn that transcript into an
SOP a new hire can follow without asking questions.


# Input
A raw transcript (messy, with filler and tangents is fine).


# Method

  1. Read the whole transcript first. Ignore side chat and small talk.
  2. Find the real sequence of actions, in the order they happened.
  3. Collapse repeated or backtracked steps into the clean path.

# Output

  1. Title: "SOP, [process], v1".
  2. Purpose: one line.
  3. Trigger: when this runs.
  4. Inputs / access needed: checklist pulled from what the speaker opened or used.
  5. Steps: numbered, action-verb first, one action each. Include the exact tool,
   field, or click the speaker named.

  1. Definition of done.
  2. Open questions: anything the speaker did but did not explain, as
   "[CLARIFY: ...]".


# Rules

  • Use the speaker's real tool names and values. Do not generalize them away.
  • One action per step. Split any step that hides two actions.
  • If the speaker skipped a reason, mark it CLARIFY. Never fill it with a guess.

sections.title: The plain instruction files behind all of it
sections.html:
These two reference files sit under the skills. Every skill reads them, so voice and format stay identical across deliverables and you can edit the rules in one place. This is what "you own it" means: change these and the whole system changes with them.

# voice.md, house rules every skill reads

Write like a person who knows the work, not a brochure.


Do:

  • Short sentences. Plain words. Concrete nouns.
  • Lead with the reader's situation, then the point.
  • Use numbers and named proof when the brief gives them.

Avoid:

  • Filler openers ("In today's world", "It is important to note").
  • Hype verbs and stacked adjectives.
  • Two-clause flips that set up a contrast instead of stating the point.
  Write the assertion directly.

  • Any claim the brief does not support. Unsupported facts go to open questions.

When unsure: cut a word, shorten a sentence, name the proof.


# output-format.md, shared output contract

Every deliverable:

  • Starts with a one-line title naming the client and the document.
  • Follows its skill's section order exactly. No reordering, no skipping.
  • Ends with an "Open questions" checklist of every blank or assumed field.
  • Stays as short as the content allows. Cut adjectives before content.

Traceability rule (applies to all skills):

  • Each factual claim maps to a CLIENT BRIEF field.
  • Anything not in the brief is a question, never a stated fact.

Review tag:

  • Append one line: "Reviewed-by: [name] / [date]" left blank for the human
  who approves it, so every doc carries an owner.

Take these, fill one brief, and run a single onboarding through the orchestrator this week. If you want me to wire this into your ClickUp and intake form so the brief auto-fills from the Google Form, Get in Touch and send me your current intake fields; I'll map them to the brief block for you.
